description: Give students with disabilities greater access to the arts, and good things happen: They come to school more often, face fewer disciplinary problems and improve their writing skills, according to new research from the University of Missouri.
title: The art of success: Study shows arts education benefits students with disabilities

description: Bats carry some of the world's deadliest viruses. Now, as climate change, extreme heat and habitat destruction intensify, so too could the risk of these diseases spreading to humans, according to new Adelaide University research.
title: Climate change and habitat loss could fuel deadly bat-borne disease

description: Could bringing back large herbivores help preserve Europe's rural landscapes and reduce wildfire risk? This is one of the key questions explored by an international study involving the University of Zaragoza, recently published in the journal Ecosystem Services.
title: Prehistoric ecosystems could hold clues to preventing future wildfires

description: Scientists at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL), Argonne National Laboratory (ANL) and Washington State University (WSU) have conducted the first dynamic compression experiments on plutonium at a national light source facility, the Dynamic Compression Sector (DCS).
title: Exquisite X-rays and dynamic compression initiate a new era of physics experiments on plutonium

description: Sales of antibiotics for use in food-producing animals have fallen by 11% in Canada since 2018, but not because of federal policy changes.
title: Policy changes in Canada had little effect on sales of antibiotics for animals, study finds

description: A mountain range can bear the marks of events from tens of millions of years ago. The challenge lies in determining when each mark was created. In southern Türkiye's Central Taurides, scientists have developed a method to date some of these ancient movements by examining tiny calcite deposits that formed as faults shifted. This new timeline alters the region's geological history. Researchers discovered a previously unrecognized period during which parts of the crust slid laterally, between the Early Eocene and Early Miocene. They also found that the region's later extension began around 25 million years ago, earlier than previously believed.
title: Ancient minerals reveal a missing chapter in Türkiye's mountain-building history

description: Solid–liquid mixing, where particles are dispersed in a liquid, is essential in many industrial processes such as slurry preparation, crystallization, precipitation, adsorption and dissolution. In such cases, effective mixing is critical for contact between particles and liquid, enabling mass transfer. Floating particles often pose a challenge in mixing because they are lighter than the liquid and tend to float at its surface. While impeller agitation does draw them into the liquid, the minimum mixing intensity needed for effective drawdown has been difficult to define.
title: New mixing benchmark could help industry reduce energy use in stirred tanks

description: Phytosterols are plant-derived compounds found in vegetable oils, nuts and seeds. They are studied for their ability to reduce cholesterol absorption, yet only about 5% enter the circulation and most are excreted. How gut bacteria influence their metabolism and tissue distribution has remained unclear.
title: Researchers trace how gut microbes transform dietary plant sterols into circulating sulfated metabolites

description: When you visit one of Norway's open-air museums, you can experience a piece of old Norway: log-built timber houses, farmsteads and farm complexes, often situated in a historic cultural landscape.
title: Should we save every old building?

description: Civil engineers looking forward to building structures on the moon need to know how ground motion from moonquakes will affect these buildings. But will ground motion models developed for Earth work well for the lunar landscape?
title: First lunar-specific ground motion model could guide seismic hazard assessments on moon

description: With El Niño winter storms rolling in, coastal communities will naturally brace for the obvious: surging high tides, pounding waves and seawater spilling over seawalls. Decades of storm coverage have encouraged us to measure climate risk by what crashes onto the shoreline.
title: Watch: Sea level rise isn't just waves—how groundwater threatens coastal cities from below

description: It's that time of year when Christmas ads start appearing, and brands offer up a slice of consumerist comfort as you curl up in front of a screen.
title: The philosophical reason AI Christmas ads leave audiences feeling cold

description: Quite a few scientific discoveries are a product of chance. You set out looking for one thing, but often end up finding something totally unexpected. In micropaleontology, the study of microscopic fossils, this is especially common. You never know what you're going to find until you start examining the samples under the microscope.
title: A 115 million‑year‑old 'algae rebellion' in Portugal's sea cliffs pushes back evolutionary timeline

description: When scientists shine a laser beam into a crystal, they typically expect a steady glow as the crystal's atoms are energized and begin to emit light. But in early 2024, while searching for something else entirely, researchers in the lab of Caltech's Andrei Faraon saw a crystal flash in a regular rhythm, like a metronome keeping a beat. The flashes came from billions of atoms embedded in the crystal. Coupled to a tiny superconducting circuit, the atoms had become synchronized and started emitting light together through a special quantum phenomenon known as superradiance.
title: Atoms in sync: Superradiance offers a new kind of frequency comb

description: We're nearing two milestones in the smartphone era. January will mark 20 years since Steve Jobs first unveiled the iPhone from a stage in San Francisco.
title: Q&A: Schools that ban cellphones see uptick in test scores

description: Electrocatalysis is key to turning renewable electricity into fuels and chemicals, and industrial electrolyzers typically operate at moderately elevated temperatures. Measuring how reaction rates change with temperature is also a powerful, yet underexplored, way to probe what controls them. Such measurements yield two quantities: an apparent activation enthalpy, reflecting the energetic cost of the reaction, and a prefactor, which is linked to the activation entropy.
title: Reading the temperature fingerprints of electrocatalytic reactions

description: The first hurdle may arise even before an application is submitted. A woman asks artificial intelligence to help her write her resume: The system chooses words, highlights qualities and builds a profile. Then another system, perhaps based on the same model, evaluates that text. If both reproduce gender stereotypes, the risk is a double filter: Bias enters the application and is reinforced by the person selecting it.
title: Even AI thinks it's a man's job: Models reveal gender bias in resumes and hiring assessments

description: The discoveries include gold jewelry, inscriptions and a finely carved gemstone, and were made at a site in Redesdale, Northumberland.
title: Archaeology students find Roman treasures on first excavation

description: Researchers recently identified a first of its kind: A star slightly less massive than the sun spiraled into and merged with a puffy supergiant star on the outskirts of our neighboring Andromeda galaxy. They nicknamed the newly single, potentially "rejuvenated" star Bao. Their discovery was then bolstered by quick-turn observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope that were carefully cross-referenced with extensive data from telescopes in space and on the ground.
title: Webb confirms first-of-its-kind merger of a supergiant and smaller sun-like star

description: Calcareous grasslands are wildflower-rich ecosystems that develop on shallow, alkaline, nutrient-poor soils over chalk or limestone bedrock. They are rare and important habitats for wild bees and other pollinators—yet how well they can support these valuable communities depends on how they are managed. An international research team, led by the University of Göttingen, has shown that long-term abandonment or intensive management threatens the diversity of wild bees. Extensive management of these areas, together with appropriate nature conservation measures in the surrounding landscape, is crucial. The findings were published in the Journal of Applied Ecology.
title: Protecting wild bees in Europe through calcareous grassland management and connected habitats

description: Cyberattacks and other harms caused by artificial intelligence challenge the ability of laws to determine who is liable. Product liability law would point to the company that built the AI model, but AIs are trained on data the company didn't produce, and the legions of people who have used them also played a role. Free speech and social media immunity laws that treat an AI agent as responsible for its own actions could imply the AI agent deserves the same rights as a person.
title: Who's to blame for a rogue AI? New legal framework maps accountability

description: A report published today from the King's Global Institute for Women's Leadership has found that young men in Britain are more likely to misperceive society's views on gender compared to other generations. Researchers found that Gen Z males are more likely to think society holds traditional views about them and therefore may be conforming to social expectations most Britons have left behind.
title: Gen Z men more likely than boomers to hold traditional views

description: With an unusual genetic modification that disabled cells' recycling systems, researchers found a way to make cells produce significantly larger amounts of the proteins used to discover and develop new medicines. The findings could help speed up drug development while reducing research and development costs.
title: Switching off cellular recycling gene increases yields of hard-to-make drug target proteins

description: One of the most important ancestors to humans was around for much longer than previously believed. That is the conclusion of a new international study published in Nature in which researchers, including scientists from the University of Copenhagen, analyzed nine fossil teeth discovered in two caves in southern China. The teeth are between 324,000 and 184,000 years old, extending the known timeline of Homo erectus by around 200,000 years.
title: One unusual tooth suggests Homo erectus shared southern China with another human species

description: During the record-breaking Pacific Northwest heat dome in 2021, a mussel's life depended on its size and location on the shoreline at Cattle Point on San Juan Island.
title: Midsize mussels fared the worst during the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome

description: Ammonia is drawing renewed attention as a "magic container" for safely storing and transporting hydrogen, a promising clean energy source of the future, as well as a carbon-free fuel that does not emit greenhouse gases when burned. However, for ammonia to be widely used as a key fuel, improving the efficiency of its production process is essential.
title: Shrinking ruthenium catalysts boosts ammonia production rate up to 57-fold

description: Photonics-based quantum computers open up new possibilities for investigating highly complex problems in mathematics and have the potential to revolutionize fields ranging from energy and chemical research to secure communications. By utilizing the unusual properties of light particles, they can perform calculations that pose enormous challenges even for the most powerful supercomputers—or remain entirely beyond their reach. At Paderborn University, researchers are now investigating a fundamental question using Germany's first scalable photonic quantum computer, a 'Gaussian boson sampler': which quantum resources are most important for the performance of these devices?
title: Scalable photonic quantum computer provides new insights into the fundamentals that shape its performance

description: The conversion of tropical rainforests into intensively farmed rubber or oil palm plantations threatens global biodiversity. However, this does not necessarily lead to the increasing similarity of the remaining species in every case, as might be expected. An international research team led by the University of Göttingen discovered that organisms react very differently to intensive agriculture. The results are published in the journal Nature.
title: Tropical plantations reshape biodiversity in ways species counts alone cannot reveal

description: A newly described crab species from the South China Sea suggests a relatively recent shift in one crab lineage from intertidal habitats to deeper waters. Found at depths of about 100–300 meters (330–980 feet), Macromedaeus putrimanubriatus is closely related to the intertidal species M. orientalis.
title: Newly described South China Sea crab suggests relatively recent shift from shallows to deeper waters

description: Electric battery-powered ferries use electricity from the shore to charge batteries on board. These batteries supply electric motors that propel the ship. On suitable routes, low-carbon electricity could make sea travel substantially cleaner and strengthen its potential as an alternative to flying.
title: Where in Europe could electric‑powered ferries create cleaner travel routes?

description: A China–Italy joint research team has reconstructed the time-resolved spectrum of GRB 221009A, the brightest gamma-ray burst (GRB) ever observed, and proposed that the burst may have produced a magnetically dominated jet with a hollow core. This is presented as a possible interpretation of the emission line's rise-then-fall evolution rather than a direct detection.
title: Spectral clues suggest hollow-core magnetic jet in brightest-ever gamma-ray burst

description: It is hard to imagine a more American holiday than Thanksgiving. Every year, elementary schoolers learn about the first celebration: that after surviving a terrible year, New England's first European immigrants, the Pilgrims, invited their Indigenous neighbors to a feast in gratitude for their help and God's providence.
title: Today's Thanksgiving holiday was invented amid the Civil War to unite a divided country

description: Lighting has evolved from simply illuminating objects to changing their perceived colors. A smart lighting technology has been developed that changes how objects appear in color by adjusting only the light shining on them, without repainting the objects or modifying their surfaces. The technology can change the perceived color of specific objects while maintaining natural white illumination in the surrounding space. Visitors will be able to see how the same object appears in different colors at an exhibition to be held at the National Science Museum in Daejeon, South Korea, in November.
title: Smart lighting technology enables remote color control

description: New research has revealed young emperor penguins encounter industrial krill fishing in their epic first year at sea, strengthening the case for proposed new marine protected areas. The study was co-led by France's CNRS, the Center Scientifique de Monaco and the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution. The international research team tracked 48 juvenile emperor penguins from three colonies around the Weddell Sea: Snow Hill Island, Jason Peninsula and Atka Bay.
title: Young emperor penguins encounter industrial krill fishing during first year at sea

description: The headlines of recent weeks and months have been dominated by men accused of doing terrible things to women.
title: Yes, men and boys should be shamed for misogyny. It's part of how we stamp it out

description: For the first time, an international research team coordinated by the IPK Leibniz Institute has characterized genomic diversity across the agriculturally important genus Hordeum. The study reveals how the genomes of barley and its wild relatives have evolved. These findings open up new avenues for systematically investigating this diversity and, in the long term, utilizing it for plant breeding. The results are published in the journal Nature.
title: Wild barley's genetic diversity opens up new avenues for research and breeding

description: Island species typically evolve in isolation—and often without many predators. As a result, islands are home to high numbers of unique species.
title: Insects on these sub‑Antarctic islands are bouncing back after invasive rats and mice were eradicated

description: Albert Einstein's ghost is trapped inside a science laboratory, and he needs help escaping. Fortunately, a group of seventh graders is up to the challenge.
title: Learning science one virtual escape room at a time

description: The usual advice for people visiting wilderness areas is to leave nothing but footprints. But as our new study shows, even footprints may disturb rare ecosystems in Antarctica and cause irreversible changes.
title: In Antarctica's ice‑free areas, even footprints can damage rare microscopic ecosystems

description: When rain falls on farmland, lawns and gardens, it can wash phosphate from fertilizers into nearby waterways, triggering harmful algal blooms that cloud lakes and rivers, release toxins and rob the water of oxygen needed to sustain aquatic life. Now, Northwestern University and Argonne National Laboratory researchers have developed a reusable electrode that captures phosphate from water in laboratory tests, potentially recovering a valuable, nonrenewable resource while reducing water pollution.
title: Electrified fabric captures phosphate for potential recovery from wastewater

description: On Sundays at Gurdwara Guru Nanaksar in Chapin, South Carolina, diners sit in rows on the floor while volunteers walk along each row carrying pots and trays of food. They pause to offer each person a spoonful of dal, a dish made with lentils, or a serving of vegetables. When the roti—a kind of flatbread—comes around, diners hold out both hands, palms up. A volunteer places the bread directly into their hands. This is "langar," the free communal meal served at Sikh houses of worship around the world.
title: As Americans gather for Thanksgiving, a centuries‑old Sikh tradition offers an expansive vision of hospitality

description: What if light could be used not just to observe matter, but to actively reprogram it? Photochromic materials contain molecules that switch between distinct molecular states when exposed to different colors of light. This ability offers exciting possibilities for optical memory and light-controlled electronic devices. However, controlling these molecular changes within extremely small spaces remains challenging because conventional optics cannot focus light to dimensions much smaller than its wavelength.
title: Using light to switch molecular states in the smallest of spaces

description: A new research study assessed five major PE packaging applications and organized the analysis around three germane, current questions. How does PE compare with paper, glass, and metal alternatives? How do reuse, post-consumer recycled content, and end-of-life recycling affect the potential environmental impact results? What happens when package-level differences scale to projected demand through 2030 and beyond?
title: A new life cycle assessment of polyethylene packaging and alternatives in the US and Europe

description: Every year, the bogong moth sets off on long migrations through the night. To find its way, it uses the stars as a guide. Now, a new study from Lund University shows that, like migratory birds, the moth also has a built-in magnetic compass that helps it stay on course.
title: Migrating moth uses Earth's magnetic field as a compass

description: Researchers have fabricated two ultrathin crystal sheets that, when stacked and rotated relative to each other, create a square lattice of defects at their interface. These defects change how electrical charges are arranged, and when the 10-nanometer-thick sheets are bonded and twisted, tiny electrical patterns emerge at the interface. These controllable arrangements could eventually prove useful in the electronics industry, although using them in a working device will require further research.
title: Crystal layers just 10 nanometers thick assemble into a tiny tunable grid

description: Some taxpayers use charitable donations to illegally reduce their taxes, using schemes orchestrated by promoters and supported by financial advisers and charities.
title: Inflated receipts and fake loans: Giving to charities to evade tax

description: The landmark Global Biodiversity Framework, agreed upon in 2022, was a major step forward in tackling global biodiversity loss. But without consistent, scientifically robust measures of progress, its ambitions risk going unrealized, a global collaboration of scientists has argued.
title: Global Biodiversity Framework at risk of becoming an empty promise

description: University of Queensland researchers have used gravity to transmit a message through a brick wall using an elevator and a sensitive gravimeter. The unusual experiment took place in UQ's Parnell Building, where the team of physicists sent the elevator back and forth between two levels, moving its 1.8 metric ton (4,000 pound) counterweight between positions representing binary 0 and 1.
title: Physicists send an unblockable message using gravity

description: University of Michigan researchers have developed a better way to understand why earthquakes occur and what size they might be. Currently, models that predict earthquakes only account for slipping that occurs along a main fault, activity that usually generates large earthquakes. Instead, the U-M researchers have built a model that considers not only the main fault action but also the activity of rocks that lie adjacent to the fault and become damaged during earthquake events.
title: Damaged rocks may help explain why small earthquakes outnumber large ones

description: How can harmful substances be removed from water? When it comes to dyes that cannot simply be filtered out, this is usually very laborious: You need substances to which the dyes attach, and then the water often has to be painstakingly centrifuged.
title: Water purification method turns old batteries into magnetic pollutant traps

description: The human genome contains tens of thousands of genes that provide instructions for making the proteins responsible for carrying out essential functions throughout the body. But those instructions may be more versatile than scientists once understood.
title: How cells use alternative genetic instructions to produce 'shadowing proteins'

description: The night sky is as good a place as any for a mystery. Back in 2002, astronomer Scott Hyman and his colleagues detected five mysterious bursts of radio waves coming from near the center of our galaxy, spaced roughly 77 minutes apart. The signals were detected again in 2003 and 2004, but then disappeared. Despite years of searching, there was no sign of their return.
title: Strange radio signals from space could come from a dead star

description: Researchers from the Institute of Applied Ecology (IAE) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences have reviewed stable nitrogen isotope techniques for tracing the sources and quantifying the production of gaseous nitrogen in soils. The review examines four approaches for distinguishing microbial pathways that produce nitrous oxide (N₂O), nitric oxide (NO) and dinitrogen (N₂).
title: Researchers review isotope methods for tracing and quantifying gaseous nitrogen production in soils

description: In people with type 1 diabetes, the immune system mistakenly identifies insulin-producing cells in the pancreas as foreign and attacks them, leaving the body unable to properly regulate blood sugar. While insulin therapy helps manage the disease, it does not stop the underlying immune attack.
title: Stem cell–derived nanoparticles modulate immune cells and help delay type 1 diabetes in mice

description: A new study has confirmed 100 bat taxa in Madidi National Park, in northwestern Bolivia, including 99 recognized species and one that may be new to science. The park is home to 68% of the bat species known from Bolivia.
title: Bolivia's Madidi National Park shelters 99 bat species, including 7 new to the country

description: A new paper by James Wilton-Ely, Ravi Singh and collaborators explores how curriculum diversification can help address the underrepresentation of minority-background scientists in chemical sciences education.
title: Making diversity count: New paper highlights overlooked scientists in the chemical sciences curriculum

description: Scientists are observing record ocean temperatures off the British Columbia coast, with temperatures spiking as much as 2.5 degrees Celsius above the long-term averages recorded at Ocean Networks Canada (ONC) seafloor observatory sites—indicating the arrival of El Niño impacts on Canada's Pacific coastline.
title: Record ocean warming hundreds of meters below B.C. coast linked to El Niño

description: Minerals are vital for bumblebee health, but too much can be harmful. For this new study, which is published in Royal Society Open Science, researchers tested how buff-tailed bumblebees (Bombus terrestris) responded to different levels of calcium, potassium, magnesium and sodium in artificial nectar.
title: Bee-lieve it or not, bumblebees have a sweet spot for salt

description: Writing is one of the most important inventions in human history. It transformed how we share knowledge, communicate and pass information from one generation to the next. But has it also changed the way we build sentences and the complexity of our languages?
title: Writing changes language less than we think

description: Frogs, salamanders and caecilians—the three groups of living amphibians—together number more than 9,000 species. On average, they are the smallest of all four-limbed vertebrates, and some are extremely small: Brachycephalus toads measure less than 7 millimeters (0.28 inches) from snout to vent. Their ancient relatives were very different animals. Most temnospondyls, the extinct group from which modern amphibians (lissamphibians) arose, were aquatic or semiaquatic predators 1 to 5 meters (3.3 to 16.4 feet) long.
title: Miniaturization found at the origin of amphibians opens new ecological territory

description: As the world works toward protecting 30% of the planet's land and sea by 2030, the study highlights why the success of marine protected areas (MPAs) depends not just on how much ocean is designated for protection, but on how these areas are planned, governed, monitored and enforced.
title: From 'paper parks' to real protection: Guide offers steps to support marine protected areas

description: A collaboration between Murdoch University researchers and veterinarians at Taronga Zoo has produced the first detailed radiographic aging guide for short-beaked echidnas, providing a practical new way to estimate the age of these iconic Australian mammals from the time they are tiny puggles through to early adulthood.
title: How old is that puggle? Scientists develop first X-ray aging guide for echidnas

description: Parenting a teenager can be difficult at times, and this can be compounded by the intense pressure some parents feel to ensure they are successfully guiding their child through their high school graduation to the next stage of their life.
title: Parents feel judged as their child transitions from high school to adulthood

description: Understanding and improving plants often requires changing what happens inside their cells. Proteins control how cells grow, respond to stress, and carry out countless other tasks. Delivering these molecular tools directly into plant cells could give researchers new ways to study those processes and engineer useful traits. But getting active proteins past the cell wall and membrane that protect each plant cell remains a major obstacle.
title: Engineered nanosyringes open a new route into plant cells

description: Long-legged, tuxedo-clad and famously noisy, the aeʻo, or Hawaiian stilt (Himantopus mexicanus knudseni), has a family life as complicated as any reality TV show. A new study led by University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa researchers, published in Ecology and Evolution, paired a decade of birdwatching with DNA sequencing to uncover a world of egg-dumping, secret infidelities and surprisingly close family ties among the newly downlisted species.
title: DNA reveals the secret lives of Hawaiʻi's aeʻo (Hawaiian stilt)

description: When a storm hits Earth, it is always a regional event. A storm might hit northern Europe, but it never expands to cover the entire continent. That is not the case on Mars. Every three or four years, a storm of such immense scale breaks out on Mars that it swallows the entire planet. Dust blocks out the sunlight, plunging the surface into darkness. That darkness spells trouble if humans are to settle on the Red Planet in the future.
title: Bouncing sand grains may explain planet-wide dust storms on Mars

description: Benjamin Barber IV, Gianluigi Giustiziero and Simon Weschle examine a little-studied form of corporate political activity: firms providing regulators with information about rivals' potential violations. The research is published in the Strategic Management Journal.
title: How firms can use political access to target rivals' violations

description: Imagine a corporate treasurer directing her company's financial network to make a $50 million wire transfer. How can the network be certain the command is coming from a secure terminal in the company's headquarters, and not a hacker's laptop across the globe?
title: Quantum physics can verify a person's location, researchers show

description: Our distant relative, Homo erectus, survived for nearly 2 million years, far longer than our species, Homo sapiens, has survived. The extinct species of archaic human spread from Africa across Asia as far as China and Java in Indonesia through grasslands and woodland savannas. Despite evidence of these achievements, our understanding of their flexibility, preferred environmental conditions, ability to adapt and even the causes of their extinction is still very limited.
title: Ancient teeth confirm Homo erectus survived in southern China's dense tropical forests

description: A small marsupial photographed by a camera trap in Colombia was identified by an AI model as a mammal whose known range does not include the country, even though the model had been told the animal was seen in Colombia. A new study in the Biodiversity Data Journal uses this kind of error as a starting point to ask whether general-purpose AI is ready for conservation work.
title: When AI misidentifies wildlife: New study maps where species identification fails

description: The plaque that builds up on teeth and the slippery coating on rocks in a stream have something in common: they're both examples of biofilms, communities of microorganisms that attach to surfaces and surround themselves with a protective layer.
title: Could locusts help detect difficult-to-treat bacterial infections?

description: Political and social polarization is becoming increasingly visible in today's democracies. In this context, an important question arises: How are our digital habits related to the way we vote?
title: New study reveals growing link between digital consumption and political preferences

description: When it comes to the ideal of female beauty, with its emphasis on slim figures and less pronounced curves, many think mass media shaped it over the past century. But is that really the case?
title: Centuries of portrait paintings reveal how female beauty ideals have changed

description: A diamond's most useful quantum properties come from defects, places where the regular arrangement of carbon atoms is broken. One of these, a nitrogen atom situated next to a vacancy caused by a missing carbon atom, has become a key component in quantum technology.
title: How electrons find their way to diamond's quantum defects

description: NASA's Voyager 1 probe, which has been traveling through space for nearly 50 years, hit a milestone distance of one light-day away from Earth on Wednesday.
title: Voyager 1 spacecraft reaches one light-day milestone

description: One of my favorite holiday memories is of a Friendsgiving my husband and I hosted in our tiny two-bedroom house in Atlanta. We didn't have a dining room. We barely had space to fit a foldout table in the living room. I think one of us sat in an office chair because we didn't have enough seating. But having our friends gather in our home, no matter how small, made me feel proud.
title: While the term 'Friendsgiving' is new, the tradition has been around for decades

description: Research led by the Archaeology Department at Durham University has revealed that Britain's first Roman capital was home to people who had traveled thousands of miles across the Roman Empire. Using an innovative new research method, the team analyzed cremated remains from 22 burials in Roman Colchester, known at the time as Camulodunum, in southeast England.
title: Ancient remains reveal Britain's first Roman capital was surprisingly diverse

description: A research team led by Dr. Youngseok Oh and Dr. Jinsu Kim of the Composites & Convergence Materials Research Division at the Korea Institute of Materials Science (KIMS), has developed an induction joining technology that enables rapid and uniform heating and bonding of carbon fiber-reinforced thermoplastic composites (CFRTPs) using a nanocomposite aerogel combining carbon nanotubes (CNTs), magnetic iron oxide (Fe₃O₄) and polyamide 6 (PA6).
title: Faster heating, stronger bonds for carbon composites

description: Mixed with water and sprayed as a fine particle film on plants, kaolin clay powder is well known in Florida for protecting citrus orchards from insects and heat stress, but how would it work on a row crop like soybeans in the Mississippi Delta?
title: Common clay shows promise for reducing soybean pests and insecticide costs

description: Can any map be colored using just four colors? That is the question behind one of the most famous problems of mathematics, dating back to 1852. Since 1976, we have known that the answer is "yes"—but how do you actually find the coloring? Now, two professors from the University of Copenhagen and DTU, together with international colleagues, have found the optimal algorithm after a decade-long obsession. The answer provides new fundamental mathematical insights.
title: Danish researchers find efficient solution to famous 174-year-old mathematical headache

description: A new study suggests that behavioral barriers are slowing the adoption of integrated pest management (IPM), a farming approach that combines biological, cultural and chemical methods to manage crop pests while reducing reliance on pesticides.
title: Knowledge gaps may stall pesticide cuts despite financial incentives, modeling suggests

description: From daytime talk shows to late-night television, politicians have long ventured beyond traditional news programs to reach voters. In the 2024 presidential election, podcasts became a new political battleground for reaching young voters, earning the election the label of the "podcast election."
title: Joe Rogan: A catalyst in the changing landscape of political media

description: Have you ever sprayed a perfume on a paper strip in a department store and loved the smell, only to find it didn't perform the same when you sprayed it on your skin? It's a common experience.
title: Why does the same perfume smell different on different people? 'Skin chemistry' explained

description: For centuries, scientists have been fascinated by critical steps in animal evolution, such as the advent of multicellularity or the ability to fly. One such evolutionary step many have heard about is vertebrate adaptation to land. Adventuring onto land is one of the best-known stories of vertebrate success, a strategy that drove their diversification.
title: How a toxin helps African lungfish survive on land

description: Post-9/11 veterans who used minimally moderated, ideologically oriented social media platforms reported greater concern about the condition of U.S. democracy and less satisfaction with the end of the war in Afghanistan than veterans who used other social media platforms or no social media at all, according to a new study by Penn State researchers.
title: Link between social media use and veterans' democracy concerns identified

description: Throughout most of 2026, fires have been burning across Indonesia, from savannas on Papua Island to peatlands on Sumatra and Borneo.
title: Indonesia may need 350 years to recover land burned in 2026 wildfires

description: When a company decides whom to hire, promote or lay off, how much of that decision should be left to artificial intelligence?
title: What happens when AI takes the human out of human resources?

description: A research team led by Professor Inseok Hwang of the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at POSTECH, including integrated MS-Ph.D. students Jeongwon Choi and Donghyeon Kang, has developed EcoTailor, a mobile planning system that suggests actionable low-carbon daily schedules tailored to users' commitments, transportation options and personal preferences.
title: Greener living? It's all in the scheduling

description: Quantum technologies, devices and systems that process, store, transfer or collect information leveraging the laws of quantum mechanics, could outperform their classical counterparts on some real-world tasks. Many of these technologies encode quantum information in qubits, which can exist in either of two basic states or a superposition of them.
title: Using a microwave link to transfer a three-level quantum state

description: Some soybean growers who plant genetically modified dicamba-resistant soybeans have no intention of spraying the herbicide. Among other reasons, they're hedging against damaging dicamba exposure arising from neighboring fields.
title: Can natural soybean varieties handle dicamba drift? New study tests promising lines

description: Researchers have shown for the first time that genomic selection—a breeding technique widely used in agriculture—could help one of Australia's most threatened frogs become more resilient to a deadly disease.
title: Genomic breakthrough offers new hope for southern corroboree frog

description: Why do some artworks stick in our minds, while others fade away soon after we view them?
title: Art experiments reveal artists' intuitive grasp of what makes images memorable

description: Chemicals found almost everywhere in modern life pose a "global and growing threat" to human health and the environment, a landmark report based on over a decade of research has warned.
title: Scientists warn of growing health threats of chemicals found everywhere

description: A sudden heat shock can be harmful to honey bees, but as a heat wave goes on, bees adapt and the high temperatures are less destructive.
title: Sudden heat spikes harm honey bees more than sustained heat, study finds

description: Researchers from the University of St Andrews have discovered that baboons the size of hominins (early human ancestors) are being preyed upon by eagles, reshaping the way scientists might think about predator–prey interactions during human evolution.
title: Eagles preying on human-sized baboons upend existing evolutionary defense theory

description: A study published in Sustainable Development that analyzed the relationship between climate change and income inequality for 23 emerging market economies from 2002 to 2022 found that greater climate pressure is positively associated with income inequality across three different inequality indicators (the Gini coefficient, the Palma ratio and the Theil index). Per capita income and institutional quality were negatively associated with inequality, whereas unemployment was positively associated with it.
title: Climate change can worsen income inequality
